findings.title: Federated recovery-code credential is never removed and codes are never consumed
findings.body: When the recovery-codes credential lives in a user storage (federated), the code-consumption logic breaks in two ways. First, line 86 calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...) with the ID of the federated credential returned by getFederatedCredentialsStream(); that ID does not exist in Keycloak's local credential store, so the call is a silent no-op and the exhausted credential is never deleted from the user storage. Second, unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (whose isValid() updates the credential to mark a code as used), there is no mechanism that consumes a code in the user storage after successful validation: the framework only calls the storage's isValid(), and nothing updates the stored credential. The net effect is that recovery codes created in user storage are single static secrets that remain valid indefinitely and can be replayed by an attacker who observed one, defeating the one-time property that recovery codes are supposed to have.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are sent to user storage via updateCredential
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the plaintext generated codes to JSON and passes them as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Whatever a user-storage provider receives it may persist as-is (as the test provider in this PR does: it stores input.getChallengeResponse() directly as credentialData). This means the security of the codes (hashing vs. plaintext storage) is delegated entirely to third-party storage implementations, whereas the local provider always stores only hashes. Additionally, the fully-populated credentialModel with hashed codes that the caller built is discarded in this branch, so the provider loses the createdDate/userLabel metadata. At minimum this contract should be documented on the method so storage implementers know they are responsible for hashing, or the hashed model should be transferred.

findings.title: getCredentials NPEs when the user is not present in the storage map
findings.body: In the new getCredentials() override, getMyUser(user) can return null (users.get(...) of an unknown username), but the code dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes without a null check. Every other method that calls getMyUser (getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) guards for null. A credential listing for a user that has been removed from the map will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which can break unrelated credential queries.

findings.title: Test does not verify that a used federated recovery code cannot be replayed
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only performs a single successful login with one recovery code and never asserts that the same code is consumed (i.e., a second login with the same code should fail, and after 12 uses the credential should be exhausted and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action re-triggered). Since the production code has no path that consumes federated recovery codes (see the finding on RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), the test as written passes while leaving the one-time-code property untested and broken. Add a replay/exhaustion assertion so this gap is caught.
